name: journal_export
description: Read a systemd journal from an evidence file or directory with journalctl (--file or --directory, never this machine's own journal) and keep every field of every entry. The complete native export (`journalctl -o json --all`) is written exactly as journalctl produced it, one entry per line, to $OUT/journal-native.jsonl when write_text is true in a job; the answer carries a projection of each entry as well: the cursor, both clocks raw (realtime and monotonic microseconds, and the source clocks) with the decoded UTC time and its fraction, the boot and machine ids, the identity fields (pid, uid, comm, exe, unit, session, identifier, priority, transport, hostname) and the line in the native file; a field journalctl wrote as a byte array is named by its length (encoding bytes) and never printed as numbers or as text, null is named as such, a string is cut at 1024 characters with its whole length (truncated_fields), a field that holds several values shows the first five and their count, and a field name or boot id longer than 128 characters is cut or counted; the native file holds every field whole. Per boot it gives the entry count and the first and last cursor and clock values. The argv is recorded as an array, time bounds must carry their own zone (a UTC suffix or @epoch: journalctl reads a bare time in this machine's zone), the stderr is kept whole in a file (the answer gives its name, its size and its sha256, never its lines, which can quote paths and entries), a deadline (max_seconds) returns what was read as partial, and a line that is not JSON, or longer than 32 MiB, is located and counted (its bytes are in the native file); a journal directory that holds links is refused, since journalctl may follow them out of the evidence; a journalctl that failed and wrote nothing is an error, and its `-- No entries --` notice (it runs with --quiet) is counted as no entries and not as a record. The path must be a regular file or a directory (a pipe is never passed to journalctl), no component of it under the working directory may be a link, and this machine's own journal is refused: a path outside the run directory whose journal files carry the machine id of this machine's /etc/machine-id in their headers (a file format field read from each file, up to 200 files, no link followed), or that is named by that id, wherever it is and however it is spelled; a path under /var/log/journal that carries another machine's id is not refused for its place. Only where this machine's id cannot be read is the place used, as /var/log/journal and /run/log/journal and what they are links to. The root directory of a file system is refused (it is not a journal), and a directory is checked for links within max_seconds and at most 100,000 entries: a directory that cannot be checked in that is refused as not a journal directory, with where the walk stopped. An earlier output of the same job (the stderr file, the verify output) is never written over: the next one is numbered. mode: verify runs journalctl --verify alone, keeps its whole output and exit code, and claims only a structural check: not that nothing is missing or removed, that the host kept a persistent journal, or that an unsealed journal is authentic. A boot id names a boot and orders nothing; within a boot the order is monotonic, because the wall clock can step. SENSITIVE: a journal holds command lines and application messages that can hold a secret; the answer carries their length, not their text, and `grep` (a pattern over the message, which would tell a caller what the message holds) is refused outside a job; in a job the answer says filter_touched_withheld_text. write_text (refused outside a job) writes the native entries to a private file, preview_text (refused outside a job) adds message and cmdline to the projection; run it as a job with secret_output: true. preview_text holds at most 64 KiB of a message per entry in the answer (preview_truncated says so; the whole is in the native file). journalctl runs in this tool's own process group, never a session of its own, so the harness ending the tool by killing its group ends journalctl with it; the deadline and a SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP end journalctl and what it started. The stop signal is the process block's: it ends journalctl and what it started, closes the text file and exits 128 plus the signal, and it prints no document of its own. A paging or text write that fails (a full disk) keeps the rows already written under the file's name, or removes its temporary, and the error answer says which. The text file holds at most 256 MiB: past it the records are counted (`not_written` in `text`), the answer is partial and the rest is in the evidence at the locators; the paging files hold at most 128 MiB together, with the same `not_written` in `pages`. The lists of the answer have fixed bounds: at most 20 links named (link_count says how many), 20 unparsable lines (parse_errors.count says how many), 5000 boots (boots_truncated) and 500 field names in the census (field_census_truncated). Every answer carries `status` (complete, partial or failed) and `status_basis`, the pair the recipes' coverage.json carries: verify mode's answer carries it too. A disk image (E01, raw, VHD(X), VMDK, QCOW2, by its first bytes, or by its name and a boot sector) is refused with the routes that read one: the catalogue's linux-target files, linux_triage, or files extracted first in a job with target-fs.  A process that journalctl left running after it exited (one that holds the pipe journalctl printed on or the stderr file, in the tool's process group or in a session of its own, or one that holds no descriptor and writes by name) is stopped, killed and reaped by the shared process block's settle() before the export and the stderr file are read, sized and hashed; one found, or a host where the absence of one cannot be proven (not Linux, PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER refused), makes the answer at most partial (program_group.left_behind, program_group.unproven and a line in problems and status_basis), and the export and the stderr file are then what the leftover had written when it was ended. A refusal carries no program_group. A process that is no descendant of the program (started through a service manager) is not found. The pipe is read to journalctl's end: a process that holds it after journalctl exited is let go after one second (and ended), where before it held the tool to max_seconds.

path.description: A .journal file, or a journal directory such as var/log/journal (a link is refused)

since.description: A time with its own zone: 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC' or '@<seconds since the epoch>'. A bare time is refused

until.description: A time with its own zone, as since

grep.description: A journalctl --grep pattern over the message. Refused outside a job (a pattern over withheld text is an oracle on it); in a job the answer says filter_touched_withheld_text

limit.description: Projected entries shown inline (default 200); all are counted and, when there are more, the whole projection is written as JSON Lines and named in pages.records.all_results

max_seconds.description: How long the call may take, the check of a directory for links included (default 240, at most 270); after it the read stops and the answer is partial, with the files named

write_text.description: SENSITIVE: Write the whole native export to $OUT/journal-native.jsonl (default false). Refused unless the tool runs as a job, which must be run with secret_output: true; a file already there is refused; the answer never carries the text (declared secret_output: a job that sets write_text is run as secret output, and the tool refuses write_text when SECRET_OUTPUT is not 1)

preview_text.description: SENSITIVE: Put message and cmdline in the projected entries of the answer (default false). Refused unless the tool runs as a job, which must be run with secret_output: true (declared secret_output: a job that sets preview_text is run as secret output, and the tool refuses preview_text when SECRET_OUTPUT is not 1)
